storm.summary_layperson: No storm risk this evening — radar is clear, there are no weather alerts, and it stays a cool, mostly cloudy, breezy night at the cove just like in the surrounding towns.
storm.local_effect_blurb: No marine-layer buffer tonight: the Sound (56°F) is already 11°F warmer than the air, and that widens to about 15°F by 7 PM as the air cools — but there is nothing on radar for it to matter.
storm.detail_html:
Regional picture: quiet. The latest radar scan (3:48 PM) shows no storm cells anywhere in the approach sector, the National Weather Service has no alerts in effect, and the atmosphere has almost no thunderstorm fuel — instability (CAPE) is about 40 J/kg and falls to zero after dark, far below the roughly 500 J/kg needed to sustain convection. Wind shear aloft is a modest 20 kt from the west-northwest, building toward 30 kt by 8 PM, but with nothing to organize it is irrelevant tonight.

Local effects: the cove's usual protection comes from cool Sound water sitting under warmer air, which forms a stable layer that starves incoming storms. In mid-November that setup is reversed. The Sound is 56°F while the air is 45°F, so the water is 11°F warmer than the air, and the gap only grows as the evening cools — about 13°F by 5 PM and 15°F by 7 PM, because the Sound holds its temperature while the air drops after sunset (4:36 PM). There is no marine-layer buffer now and none develops during the window.

Sea breeze: not in play. Only 1 of 20 coastal stations shows any southerly wind; the whole region is under a west-northwest background wind, and the sun is already setting, so there is no thermal engine to start one.

Most likely outcome: a dry, mostly cloudy, chilly evening at the cove — mid-40s at 4 PM falling to around 40°F by 7–8 PM — with the same weather as Stamford, Port Chester, and inland Greenwich. Tonight the cove behaves no differently from its neighbors.

What would change the call: very little inside this window. It would take new showers appearing on radar to the west or northwest, and even then the lack of instability points to light rain rather than thunder. With no Sound buffer in place, anything that did arrive would reach the cove at face value.

wind.regime_label: Moderate gradient wind — no sea breeze in play

hourly.shift_note: steady W–WNW, puffy off the land

wind.tactics_blurb: A moderate westerly background wind holds all evening at 7–9 kt with gusts 10–14 — it does not die with the sunset. More pressure sits on the open-water (south) side of the course, and the slow drift from WNW toward W favors the left; work the left on the beat and expect holes close to the Connecticut shore.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
The call: a moderate gradient wind — no sea breeze in play. A sea breeze needs the land to be at least 5°F warmer than the water; today the air is 45°F against a 56°F Sound, an air–water temperature difference of −11°F, so there is no thermal at all. What is blowing is the large-scale background (gradient) wind: the airport-grade stations average 8.7 kt, the regional median direction is WNW 299°, and Riverside YC reads WNW 303° at 10 kt gusting 12 (10-minute average 8 kt).

Will it hold? Yes. Sunset is at 4:36 PM, before the window even opens, and a gradient wind does not depend on the sun. The high-resolution model keeps 7–9 kt from 5 PM through 8 PM with a small peak near 6 PM, and the usual after-dark settling of the lower atmosphere should only take a knot or so off and trim the gusts. Expect 7–9 kt with gusts 10–14 throughout.

Direction and shifts: the wind starts W to WNW (280–290°), then backs slowly left to due west (about 262°) by 7–8 PM. That is a gradual, one-way trend rather than a back-and-forth oscillation, with a short swing right around 6 PM on the way. On top of the trend, wind coming off the land to the west and northwest is puffy — expect gust-and-lull cycling with 10–15° swings in the puffs.

Where the pressure sits: a westerly is channeled down the Sound from the New York direction, so it is stronger out in open water and patchy near the Connecticut shore. The Western Sound buoy shows this clearly — 16.5 kt gusting 24 mid-Sound against 10 kt in the cove. On a beat to the west, the left side is the open-water side toward the cove mouth, and it also gains as the wind backs left. The right side, tucked under the western shore, will have the holes.

What it feels like: 7–9 kt is the comfortable range for one-design dinghies — good racing breeze, not overpowering, with gusts to the low teens keeping it lively. Outside the cove it is a different day: mid-teens gusting into the 20s on the open Sound. It is cold and fully dark, with air near 40°F by 7 PM.

Model check: the model's 4 PM direction (285°) is within 8° of the observed stations (293°) — good agreement, and since this is a gradient-wind day rather than a sea-breeze day, the sea-breeze direction correction does not apply. The model's 7.5 kt matches Riverside YC's 10-minute average of 8 kt. Station directions agree fairly well (75% within 45° of the median), with the scatter coming from sheltered backyard stations reading under 3 kt.

data_caveats: HRRR 20Z run had only posted through 8 PM at publish time — the 9 PM and 10 PM wind rows are carried forward from 8 PM, not modeled
Gust values are estimated from Riverside YC's and the Western Sound buoy's current gust-to-average ratios (no model gust field)
